name: Missing-data handling: -200 fill as NaN in per-scan rasters, stacks and AIA cutouts
note: Verdict, effort and milestone hold: glue-solar code alone on released core 1.27.0 + irispy 0.9.0, and M0 lists '-200 fill' as a blocker. The approach and risk (1) need correcting. (a) -199 should count as missing by default, and the claim that it is 'probably the saturation flag' is contradicted by the evidence. IRIS-SSW treats -199 as missing: iris_make_fits_level3 v1.29 'treats also -199 as missing' and NaN-fills r < -198.5, and iris_raster_browser uses missing=[-200.,-199.]. The F164 feature text itself says '-200/-199'. L2 saturation is the top int16 code 32760, which scales to 16182 DN (iris_getwindata: 'Saturated data seem to be set at 16183 DN'), not -199. (b) Match the exact codes with np.isin(values, (-200, -199)), not '< -198.5'. The irispy *_test.fits fixtures are float and hold many genuine values below -200, so a threshold would wipe them. (c) irispy fills only -200 in SJIs, so the loader must also fill -199 there. That is an in-place write on the float SJI and needs no copy. Leave 16182 (saturated) alone, because Level-3 and CRISPEX keep it. Restricting -199 to IRIS instruments and not AIA is optional, since AIA -199 is unverified. On real data, SJI masks will then differ from cube.mask; the fixtures contain no -199, so test_importer.py:112 still passes. The user should still confirm the -199 default, but the plan should state that SSW treats -199 as missing rather than suggesting it is saturation. The other claims check out: irispy flips raster data but not the mask, compute_statistic uses finite=True, and the Profile viewer uses the default finite=True.
approach: WP10, in glue_solar/sources/loaders/iris.py::_cube_data. Mark samples as missing where the data equal irispy.utils.constants.BAD_PIXEL_VALUE_SCALED (-200), taking this from the data rather than from cube.mask. Convert with values.astype(np.result_type(dtype, float32), copy=False) and set values[missing] = nan, only when any sample is missing. Integer AIA cutouts without fill stay int16, and float SJIs, which irispy has already NaN-filled, are not copied. In stack_spectrograms.py:53-62, replace the cube.mask copy with 'output[i] = cube.data; output[i][output[i] == BAD] = nan', which also removes one per-scan copy. The #53 layer_artist_maker (sources/iris.py:31-44) then renders these samples transparent. glue's percentile, Min/Max and Profile statistics already skip non-finite values (compute_statistic finite=True). I applied the complete patch to a scratch copy, 1 file per concern: scratchpad/feas-data-quality/patch.diff. Only -200 counts as missing; see the risks for -199.
upstream: None, because it runs on released core 1.27.0 and irispy 0.9.0. As an optional nice-to-have, ask irispy to NaN-fill float raster data as it already does for SJIs (io/sji.py:249-251); the loader does not depend on it.
risks: (1) -199 is not treated as missing. Real files contain a spike of exact -199.0 values with almost no neighbours at -198.75 (SJI 1400: 1905 at -199.0 versus 2 at -198.75), and they sit inside very bright kernels: the median of the 3x3 neighbourhood maxima is 6515 DN against an image median of 44. ITN26 says saturated pixels are flagged as Inf, and int16 L2 files cannot store Inf. So -199 is probably the saturation flag. That is my inference and not documented. Turning it into NaN would make saturated cores transparent, so the user must decide whether -199 means +Inf (saturated) or missing, or should be left alone. (2) The in-place NaN write (copy=False) changes the irispy cube array. That is safe today because the cube is discarded, but a future caller that keeps the cube would see the change. (3) Downstream code must be NaN-aware: WP2 moments and WP6 fits (wp6_fitting.py:61 nan_to_num). (4) An integer AIA cutout that does contain fill doubles in memory when converted to float32. None of the 9 local AIA cutouts contains -200, so the AIA fill path is not checked on real data. (5) Tested contracts are unchanged: the patched suite passes.
reuse: The existing stack NaN logic (glue_solar/sources/loaders/stack_spectrograms.py:53-56@157cf44) is generalised in scratchpad/feas-data-quality/patch.diff. No WP prototype is needed.
evidence: Current state: 4000005156 r00000 C II per-scan has n(-200)=2504368 (10.8%) and NaN=0; glue Min/Max gives (-200, 1728.75) and 99.5 gives (-200, 23.25). After NaN-filling: Min/Max (-153.75, 1728.75), 99.5 (-7.0, 24.69), 99.8 (-7.52, 31.5). The whole-map Mean profile from glue compute_statistic differs by more than 1 DN at 465 of 468 wavelength pixels (at most 199.3 DN). 46144 of 49344 spectra are partly missing and 3200 fully (probe1.log, probe2.log). With the patched scratch loader on real data: V34 NaN positions equal the flipped raw -200 exactly, no -200 is left, and C II 99.5 limits are [-7.0, 20.14] (probe5.log). Suite: patched copy 35 passed, 1 skipped (34+1 from baseline, plus my import-path check test_where), in patched_suite.log. name: IRIS_HISTO_OPT histogram-optimisation scaling
note: Verdict, M effort and M1 hold. F061 is a 'must' and WP11 is M1/M2; the M0 part is the F164 fill plus percentile=99.5 in the preset. Two points are confirmed: the per-state percentile choices fail session restore, and Custom limits round-trip. All the named hooks exist in the released versions: viewer_tool, Tool.menu_actions (the glue-qt 0.4.2 toolbar builds a QMenu from it), DropdownTool/SimpleToolMenu, and compute_statistic(percentile, random_subset). Correct the core approach: compute the limits from the displayed image, not the whole cube. BaseImageLayerState.get_sliced_data() exists in 1.27.0 and returns exactly the displayed 2-D slice, so np.nanpercentile(slice, [100*c, 100*(1-c)]) reproduces IRIS_HISTO_OPT's per-image semantics exactly. It also removes the random-subset risk, which is larger than stated: the whole-cube 10k-sample estimate is biased even at the 1e-3 IRIS default, not only at 1e-4. A 'follow slider' option is a callback on viewer_state.slices that re-applies the limits. The helper then sets v_min/v_max, which switches to Custom and stays session-safe.
approach: M0 precondition: the F164 NaN fill. With it, the built-in 99.5 preset gives sensible limits, so the M0 quicklook preset can set percentile=99.5 on the viewers it creates. For M1 (WP11), use Custom limits rather than new combo choices: a helper histo_opt_limits(data, cid, cutoff) calls data.compute_statistic('percentile', ..., 100*cutoff and 100*(1-cutoff), random_subset=10000) and sets layer.state.v_min/v_max, which switches percentile to 'Custom'. Expose it as a glue-solar toolbar tool with a cutoff menu (1e-2, 1e-3 IRIS default, 1e-4 CRISPEX default), registered through glue.config.viewer_tool and added to ImageViewer.tools in glue_solar/__init__.py setup(), following FrameTimeTool in glue_solar/tools.py. The quicklook preset calls the same helper when it creates viewers. Do NOT extend ImageLayerState.percentile choices per state from the layer_artist_maker: a session saved with percentile=99.8 fails to restore.
upstream: None for the Custom-limits tool. An optional glue-core PR could add 99.9/99.8/99.98 to the percentile choices (glue/viewers/image/state.py:537, identical on origin/main dae530c3); no such issue exists (gh search). Gamma (F062) is a separate item.
risks: glue computes percentiles over the whole cube from 10k random samples, while IRIS_HISTO_OPT/CRISPEX clip per displayed image, so limits do not follow the slider. Per-frame limits would need a slice callback in the tool. Setting limits in a layer_artist_maker would overwrite limits restored from a session, because the maker runs after state restore; for that reason only an explicit tool or the preset should set them. With a 10k sample, 1e-4 tails rest on about 1 sample, so they are noisy; use a larger random_subset for 99.98.

note: Holds on released core. coerce_numeric turns bool into int64 and leaves uint8 alone, and np.isnan works on the big-endian int16 AIA arrays, so Component(np.isnan(values).view(np.uint8)) is a one-line change that meets the 'mask dtype' M0 blocker. Keeping the component rather than dropping it matches test_importer.py:109-112, :136, :159 and :171-180. name: Time linking (nearest) fails on negative-step rasters with descending step times
note: Verdict, effort and milestone hold. The fix is in the solar port of nearest, and link_time uses only ComponentLink, which is in released 1.27.0. The risk statement is wrong: the stable argsort does not map ties to the first original index. When the lower neighbour has duplicate times, searchsorted(side='left') makes r[i-1] the last duplicate, so the index among equal times is inconsistent. The chosen time is always correct. Use u, first = np.unique(ref, return_index=True), search u, and return first[idx]. It is the same size, gives first-index semantics, and still handles descending and non-monotonic stack ravels. Keep the NaT, empty and 1-D checks. Add a duplicate-time case and a descending-time case to the acceptance test. The descending V34 behaviour is reconfirmed on real data.
approach: WP4 M0 time sync. In the glue-solar port of IRIS_PLAN_PROTOTYPES/wp4_common.py::nearest (target a new glue_solar/sources/links.py, or next to link_hpc in loaders/iris.py), remove the sorted-reference check. Compute order = np.argsort(ref, kind='stable'), run searchsorted on ref[order], and return order[idx]. Keep the NaT/empty/1-D checks and the 'ties to the earlier time' rule. link_time needs no change: line 62 passes the unsorted raster times as ref, and for a 4D V34 stack ravel() is non-monotonic even across scans, so argsort is the general fix rather than reversing.
upstream: none
risks: With duplicate reference times (multi-exposure rasters, followup-4-9/F116), the stable argsort maps a tie to the first original index. That is deterministic, but document it. The acceptance test needs a descending-time case. There is no V34 fixture in the irispy data, so build one synthetically, or with a real-data test skipped when ~/DATA is absent.
reuse: IRIS_PLAN_PROTOTYPES/wp4_common.py:37-50 nearest and :57-70 link_time; patched nearest in scratchpad/feas-data-quality/probe1.py

The patched nearest equals a brute-force argmin for the single scan (64 refs, unsorted) and for the 2-scan stack ravel (128 refs, unsorted). The current check at wp4_common.py:43 rejects both cases ('times must be finite and reference times sorted', per followup-4-1). irispy 0.9.0 io/spectrograph.py:258-259 (times = t_obs[::-1]).

name: Negative-step rasters: mask, stack NaNs and per-step meta not flipped by irispy
note: Holds. irispy 0.9.0 flips the data and times but builds the mask from the unflipped HDU, and it leaves per-step meta unflipped. Deriving missing samples from the flipped data (F164) makes the mask and NaN positions correct for any irispy version, including a future one that NaN-fills rasters or flips masks. This still holds with -199 added. The meta check, where the WCS longitude at step 0 is compared with Tx[0] and Tx[-1], was reconfirmed. A simpler deterministic gate is STEPS_AV < -0.01 and 'flipped' not in meta: the unmerged irispy fix sets meta['flipped'] and flips the arrays. That depends on the key name shipping, so the WCS check is the safer default. Only exposure time matters for M0. In 3400109360 it is constant (7.9991-7.9992 s), so the flip affects the display only in AEC-varying observations; a synthetic test is needed. revert_v34 is not a good default, as stated. No unreleased PR is required.
approach: (a) The mask and NaN positions need no version gate. The F164 change derives missing samples from the already-flipped data (values == -200) in _cube_data and stack_spectrograms, so it is correct whichever irispy is installed; cube.mask is no longer read, and the published mask is isnan(values) as uint8. (b) Per-step meta (exposure time, exposure FOV center, OBS_VRIX, OPHASEIX) matters only when glue-solar publishes it, e.g. a raster 'Exposure time' component for the M0 exposure-time display. Reverse those arrays with a version-independent check, in the same glue_solar/sources/loaders/iris.py helper: meta_unflipped = abs(Tx[0] - wcs_lon(step 0)) > abs(Tx[-1] - wcs_lon(step 0)). Alternatively gate on the irispy version (<= 0.9.0) and use the data check as the acceptance test. (c) Do not use irispy revert_v34=True as the default. It makes everything consistent, but the map comes out mirrored relative to the SJI and the steps reversed. (d) WP2 moments are fixed by (a).
upstream: Not blocking. WP0 should file an irispy issue and PR so that V34 flips the mask, uncertainty and per-step meta. The unmerged irispy branch gwcs_raster_clean:147-185 already does this and sets meta['flipped']. Upstream LM-SAL main 34b5805 (2026-09-21) and v0.9.0 (2026-09-10) are unchanged, and no issue or PR on this exists (gh search).
risks: The irispy uncertainty is also unflipped, which is harmless while the loader passes uncertainty=False and must be fixed if uncertainties are ever loaded. The meta check assumes the XCENIX FOV centre tracks the slit's WCS longitude; it held to 0.01 arcsec on both probed files. Without a V34 fixture in CI, regressions are caught only by a synthetic test or a data-gated test.

name: Thread-safety crash: glue-qt Profile ComputeWorker and GUI-thread WCSAxes share one irispy -TAB WCS
note: The verdict, effort and milestone stand, and all of it works on the released stack. One fix to the approach: use threading.RLock, not threading.Lock. With a module-level Lock, a _GlueWCS that wraps SlicedLowLevelWCS(<another _GlueWCS>) deadlocks: the outer call holds the lock and the inner call tries to take it again. Derived data such as moment, fit or export maps, or a session loader, can build that nesting. Today's prototypes avoid it only by unwrapping ._wcs first. RLock costs nothing extra. Add to the risks: wp2_moments_proto.py:29,171 passes data.coords._wcs directly into SpectrogramCube, so it uses the WCS on the GUI thread without the lock. The glue-qt histogram viewer is also threaded (glue_qt/viewers/histogram/layer_artist.py @0.4.2). It reaches the WCS the same way through data[cid], so the lock covers it. Other reads of WCS attributes stay unlocked, as the item already says; fitswcs.py:326 axis_types triggers wcsset.
approach: In glue_solar/sources/loaders/iris.py, add a lock to _GlueWCS: `_WCS_LOCK = threading.Lock()` and wrap pixel_to_world_values, world_to_pixel_values and the axis_correlation_matrix property in `with _WCS_LOCK:`. Every glue path goes through _GlueWCS: WCSAxes via SlicedLowLevelWCS on the GUI thread, and the ComputeWorker through data[x_att] -> coordinate_helpers.pixel2world_single_axis. A module-level lock is simpler than a per-instance one, and it also covers derived datasets that share the same astropy WCS object; the WP6 prototype passes data.coords._wcs to its fit maps. Its known limit is that it serialises all IRIS WCS calls; switch to per-WCS locks only if contention is measured. A per-thread deepcopy of the wrapped WCS also works (0.1 ms per copy) but has more moving parts. Ship two regression tests. (1) A CI subprocess test on the bundled irispy fixture: two Python threads call pixel_to_world_values/axis_correlation_matrix on one _GlueWCS 20000 times, and it passes if the process exits 0. (2) A manual M0 gate: the real-data Qt stress test_race.py (0 crashes in 10 consecutive runs).
upstream: none for M0. WP0: track astropy#19174 (OPEN, 'Thread-unsafe access to wcslib in astropy.wcs.WCS'). Report that wcslib tabx2s writes tabprm p0/delta scratch fields (astropy cextern/wcslib/C/tab.c:1237-1247 on main) while astropy releases the GIL.
risks: Code that reaches the astropy WCS without going through _GlueWCS is not protected, for example irispy cube.wcs used from a worker or the WP6 raw_wcs; route it through data.coords or deepcopy it. Other WCS attribute reads are not locked, and none crashed in 18 locked runs. While the GUI thread redraws WCSAxes (up to 0.06 s after the latency fix) the worker waits. The index-free WCS of the latency fix alone hides the race in the Qt stress test (4/4 survived) but not in the unit test (4/4 crashed), so the lock is required. Test only in a subprocess, because a failure kills the interpreter.

name: Slider latency grows linearly with exposure index (-TAB pixel_to_world)
note: Confirmed. Three implementation notes. (1) Check isinstance(wcs, astropy.wcs.WCS) before calling to_header(). The prototype without_step_index raises AttributeError on the SJI gwcs, so a bare call in _cube_data would break SJI loading; fixes.py only avoided this with a hasattr(wcs, 'wcs') check. (2) The rebuild costs 1.4 ms per scan, which is negligible even for 99 scans. (3) Cross-WP: the WP3 session-saver prototype (IRIS_PLAN_PROTOTYPES/sess_proto_savers.py:18-19) reads hdr['PS{ax}_2'] for both axes, so it would raise KeyError on the index-free WCS. WP3 must skip index columns that are absent.
approach: Root cause: irispy 0.9.0 writes the exposure -TAB index as an explicit identity column 1..N (irispy/io/spectrograph.py:79,83,105-108 PS3_2='RASTER'), and wcslib tabx2s searches index vectors linearly (tab.c:1169/1209), so each point costs O(exposure index). With no index vector wcslib takes psi directly, which is O(1) (tab.c:1120-1122). M0 workaround in glue_solar/sources/loaders/iris.py: add `_without_step_index(wcs)` (about 15 lines). It rebuilds the FITS WCS from wcs.to_header() minus PS3_2, plus a BinTableHDU of tab.coord and the 2-node SPATIAL index. It keeps the original WCS unless a few probe points match to 1e-12. Call it in _cube_data before wrapping in _GlueWCS, and in stack_spectrograms.py:36 on target_wcs before CompoundLowLevelWCS (:73). Remove it once irispy ships the fix. note:
The mechanism holds on released core 1.27.0 + Qt 0.4.2 and I confirmed it again on real data. The item is too optimistic in four places:
(1) The pairing rule is wrong for NUV windows. It requires 'identical Time', but in irispy 0.9.0 FUV times are aux+EXPTIMEF/2 while NUV times come from the source filenames. Mg II k differs from Si IV by about -0.06 s, so _same_grid is False. On a spatial raster, where time_axes is (), the Mg II spectrogram would therefore never follow the step. Pair on observation_key + same raster file + shape[:-1] (or Time within half a step cadence) instead.
(2) Real data crashed. On the first Pixel press with a Profile viewer open, the process aborted (the followup-2-1 WCS thread race). It ran once I added a _GlueWCS lock, so the WP10/WP1 WCS lock is a hard M0 prerequisite for this item.
(3) Latency is measured, not unknown, and it is far over budget:
  - The prototype takes about 1.05 s per drag step against 58 ms for native Pixel.
  - About 0.6 s of that is prototype waste: time_axes() evaluates the world grid before it checks STEPS_AV, and it does this on every apply. Check STEPS_AV first and cache per dataset.
  - The remaining ~0.4 s is glue's own work: every follower slider change resets WCSAxes (about 0.2 s per follower). That is the WP10 '-TAB slider latency' blocker, and a 0 ms QTimer does not remove it.
(4) The Profile viewer on real-size windows also needs the followup-2-5 fix for the large-data modal.
Smaller points:
  - 4D scan narrowing is not implemented in coord_proto (only in _retarget_point when a non-raster master is set); run_d built the narrowed state by hand.
  - F134 is covered only as a lambda-t viewer whose slit slider is set; the time/lambda markers are M1.
  - Process note: one text edit of my scratch probe ran through /usr/bin/python3 by mistake. Every probe ran in 'iris-plan'.
approach: Add glue_solar/coordination.py with one Coordinator(HubListener) per DataCollection. Store it as an attribute on the DataCollection, not as a WeakKeyDictionary value, because a value that references its key pins that key. The Coordinator subscribes to SubsetUpdateMessage and SubsetCreateMessage. A group sends one message per dataset, so it acts only on the message whose subset.data is the state's reference_data. Add a new viewer tool 'solar:coordinate' to glue_solar/tools.py, next to solar:frame_time, and append it to ImageViewer.tools in glue_solar.setup(). The tool's __init__ registers its viewer with the coordinator and hooks the state's 'slices' and 'reference_data' callbacks. Tool.close, which window_closed fires, unregisters it. On a PixelSubsetState the coordinator reads slices[i].start to get step, slit and scan. It then sets the non-displayed leading and slit axes, never the last (wavelength) axis, in every registered Image viewer that shows the same dataset or a dataset with the same step/slit grid and identical Time (the other spectral windows of one raster). The spectrum stays the native Mean profile of the Pixel subset. On a 4D stack the coordinator narrows the point's scan slice to the current or master scan. Read slider values with getattr(s, 'center', s), because 1.27.0 sliders can hold an AggregateSlice.

name: Master time selection (raster / SJI master)
note:
Verdict, effort and milestone hold. STEPS_AV is available through data.meta in the loader (main iris.py:76 sets data.meta = cube.meta), and the Time component is already a broadcast view (main iris.py:79-84), so exposure_times is cheap. Implementation notes:
- time_axes must check STEPS_AV before it computes the lon grid and must be cached per dataset. The prototype order costs about 0.2 s per call on real sns data (see the selected-point item).
- A plain Tool's 'Time master' click goes through BasicToolbar.active_tool, which deactivates that viewer's active mouse mode (for example Pixel). Document this, or make it a subtool (see the cursor-lock item).
- On negative-step (v34) rasters irispy reverses Time along the step axis (spectrograph.py:258-260), so Time decreases with index. match() is only used on scan/SJI/sns axes, where the order is ascending, so the design is safe. Keep the WP10 recheck.
approach:
The coordinator keeps one 'master' tool. By default it is the first registered viewer whose data has exposure times; the 'Time master' toolbar button of 'solar:coordinate' changes it, and the master's status bar says 'time master'. There are only two inputs: the master's 'slices' and the Pixel point.
- Master time is Time at the master's non-displayed leading slices. When the master displays the step axis (a raster map), the representative step is the selected point's step, or mid-raster with no point. This is the F112 default; the knob comes later.
- Time axes per dataset: the SJI frame axis, the stack scan axis, and the raster step axis only for sit-and-stare (raster meta STEPS_AV == 0). A spatial 3D raster has no time axis, so it only shows its offset.
- With a non-raster master, the point's time axis is moved to the matched index, so the spectrum follows time at a fixed slit: sit-and-stare step, stack scan.
- An SJI master past the raster span is handled by the no-match policy (see the sync item).

name: Coordinator lifecycle: late viewers, closed viewers, session restore, no feedback loops
note:
Confirmed. ToolbarInitializer runs initialize_toolbar after cls(session, state=...) for restored viewers, and Tool.__init__ connects window_closed -> close, which BaseQtViewerWidget.closeEvent emits. One risk is mis-stated: the hub's weak references are a requirement, not a mitigation. The hub keeps only weak references to bound handlers, so the coordinator must be held strongly (as the DataCollection attribute the item proposes) or it silently stops receiving messages. Minor points:
- Make unregister idempotent. A second call raises ValueError (seen when I detached tools by hand).
- On restore the default master is re-picked, so followers may re-sync away from the saved slider positions until WP3 persists the master.

Registration happens in the tool's __init__. glue-qt runs that for every viewer, including restored ones, because ToolbarInitializer runs after cls(session, state=restored_state). So there is no need to wrap app.new_data_viewer as wp4_common does.

- No feedback loops: there are only two inputs (the followed Pixel subset and the master's 'slices'). Every write happens under a _busy flag and only when the value differs, and follower 'slices' callbacks are ignored.
- The master choice and tolerance are persisted in M1 (WP3). IRIS-data sessions themselves are WP3 (M1).

- Master and tolerance are not saved in M0.
- IRIS sessions need WP3's savers.
- The hub subscription must end with the application. Hub uses weak references, which mitigates this.
- Qt tool-construction order may change in future glue-qt releases.

note: The released APIs exist. The marker plus Navigate work as claimed. Navigate writes the wavelength slice into every Image viewer of the dataset, including lambda-t and spectrogram viewers where wavelength is a displayed axis. That write is harmless: the lambda-t image is unchanged. So viewers only diverge through their own sliders. The preset can open Options on Navigate through the public toolbar tool, because MODES[0] is 'navigate'. Correction to the 'could move into M0' remark: in M0 the loader's wavelength is native metres, and the skeleton puts WP1's Angstrom conversion in M1. An M0 preset that follows D3 by setting x_display_unit=Angstrom would make released Navigate jump to the wrong slice. The patch is gated by behaviour: it installs only while orig('x_display_unit') == orig('x_att'), and it is idempotent (marker attribute). When core changes the priorities, the patch stops installing. name: Image layers with sunpy colormaps cannot be restored
note: The one-line registration fix works end to end. The layer cmap becomes 'irissji1400', the session restores, and the restored style-editor combo shows 'IRIS SJI 1400', which the item had left unverified. maps.py:30 (preferred_cmap=scan_map.cmap) hits the same failure for AIA/HMI today, and the same line fixes it. Core #2597 (OPEN) only serialises the style's preferred_cmap, not the layer cmap. One cosmetic caveat, already present today: sunpy has cmaps with identical lookup tables (goes-rsuvi171 == sdoaia171, irissji1330 == irissjiFUV, irissji2832 == suit_nb05, and others). The combo matches by ==, so an AIA 171 layer snaps to the first equal entry in sorted order and is labelled GOES-R SUVI. It still restores, because every registered name is a matplotlib registry key.
approach: In glue_solar/__init__.py setup(), register matplotlib's named copies instead of sunpy's objects: 'for key, ctable in cmlist.items(): colormaps.add(ctable.name, matplotlib.colormaps[key])'. The layer's cmap.name then becomes a registry key such as 'irissji1400', which core's _load_cmap can find. Add an app-level save/restore test with an SJI image viewer. Optionally, a core PR can make _load_cmap fall back to glue's colormap registry.
